answer.exemplar: A liquid boils when the saturated vapour pressure of its own vapour equals the pressure of the gas above it, so raising that pressure above the liquid raises the temperature at which the two match. While the water boils at the new, higher temperature, the energy supplied goes into the latent heat of vaporisation, freeing molecules from their neighbours, so the temperature stays fixed as the liquid disappears.

answer.exemplar: The first law only demands that energy balance, and a cycle that returns to its initial state can show no change in internal energy while the heat taken in equals the work done, so the account closes perfectly well. The second law forbids it, because the Kelvin-Planck clause says no cyclic device can have the sole effect of extracting heat from one reservoir and converting it entirely into work. Such an engine must reject heat to a second reservoir, so its efficiency stays below one.

answer.exemplar: Heat flows spontaneously from the hotter body to the colder one until no difference remains, and the second law fixes that direction, so neither body can end hotter than it started. The final value is set by conservation of energy, since the energy the block loses as it cools is exactly the energy the water gains. With their masses and specific heats known, the common temperature is the one that balances the two, weighted towards whichever body has the greater heat capacity.
